images.text: If you had realized what went into a film or TV show you might have looked at it differently. If you had been on the set with the production team you may have been shocked to see how much they support the director. If you had witnessed an action scene being filmed, you may have realized that actors acknowledge that stunt people are incalculable.

More and more productions have started to feature special effects. This never used to be the case. They used to be far more difficult to present. As technology became available, the directors would put in more stunts. This changed everything. The stunt school was born.

In the past, stunt people would learn the ropes on the job. At first they may have been cast because of their athletic ability. They might have had some special skill. They could have come from a stunt family. That means that they have followed in a parent's footsteps.

Today stunt actors are groomed at schools. They graduate after they learn to do numerous stunts convincingly and safely. They are beyond lucky if they never get hurt. Stunt people may have been more reckless and daring yesterday, but today they're not.

If you'd been on the set of a big action film, you might have heard that the stunt coordinator used to be a famous stunt person themselves. Planning stunts is key. Most have been choreographed as carefully as ballets. That way no one got hurt. Stunt school anyone?

Talking Hypothetically and Speculating About the Past

You can use modals to talk about degrees of certainty and speculate about things in the past.
You use them to describe what is definite, probable, possible, or impossible from the speaker's point of view.

You use could have and would have to talk about things that were possible in the past and may or may not have happened (to speculate).
You often use these structures with the third conditional.
You can use must, may, might, and could to describe degrees of certainty.
You can use modals with the Present Perfect tense to talk about the possibility of a past event that is not clear in the present context.

Example:
If you had realized what went into a film or TV show you might have looked at it differently.
  • May have has a slightly stronger meaning than might have or could have.
  • You can add not to make a negative speculation (It may not have been true).

You use could have to talk about possibilities if something had been different in the past.
For example:
They could have come from a stunt family.

You use would have to imagine a result if something had been different in the past.
For example:
That means they would have followed in a parent's footsteps.
If you had been on the set with the production team, you may have been shocked to see how much they support the director.
If you had witnessed an action scene being filmed, you may have realized that actors acknowledge that stunt people are incalculable.
If you'd been on the set of a big action film, you might have heard that the stunt coordinator used to be a famous stunt person themselves.

Talking About the Past: The Present Perfect tense vs. The Simple Past tense, Used to and Would

You use the Present Perfect tense to talk about a past action or an action that began in the past that is connected to the present in some way.
You use the Simple Past tense to talk about many kinds of past events: short, quickly finished actions, longer situations and repeated events.
You use used to and would to talk about past habits which are now finished. There is an idea that circumstances have changed. You do not use it to talk about what happened at a past time.

You can use the Present Perfect tense to talk about experience.
When you use the Present Perfect tense, you think about the past and present together. There is some connection between what happened in the past and now.
For example: I have learned English. = I learned English in the past and now I can speak English.
Usually, when you use the Simple Past tense, the time of the finished action is clear from the context or explicitly mentioned in the sentence.
For example: Yesterday, I went to the store.
It is clear when the action occurred. In this sentence we would not use the Present Perfect. (Yesterday, I have been to the store).
Both used to and would talk about past habits which no longer exist, but there are a couple of things to note about the usage of these expressions.

1. Would cannot be used to talk about past states. You must use used to.
For example: I used to have a dog. I would have a dog.

2. You use used to to talk about regular, important habitual behavior.
For example: I used to smoke. I would smoke.
